answer.sourceLine: Branson wrote these two sentences himself, in a post titled “Why money is like manure” published on his Virgin.com blog on 13 February 2014 — the wording is confirmed word-for-word in the archived page. The analogy is not his, though: he credits Thornton Wilder in the very next sentence, and the comparison was already in print in Francis Bacon’s Essays.

source.excerpt: If you are lucky enough to have it, then money is like manure. … If you let money pile up, it starts to stink. But if you spread it around then it can do a lot of good.
trail: 1625 — Francis Bacon’s Essays, in “Of Seditions And Troubles”: “And money is like muck, not good except it be spread” (Project Gutenberg ↗). The 1625 date is Quote Investigator’s.
1954 — Thornton Wilder gives Dolly Levi the manure line in The Matchmaker, Act 4 (Wikiquote ↗). Quote Investigator records it being quoted in a January 1956 LIFE review of the play.
16 June 1961 — Time quotes Clint Murchison Jr. relaying his father’s advice, in the “stinks like hell” wording (TIME archive ↗).
13 February 2014 — Richard Branson posts “Why money is like manure” on Virgin.com, with the exact wording quoted today and a credit to Wilder (archived page ↗).
source.excerptNote: The next sentence in the post is Branson’s own citation: he quotes Thornton Wilder’s “money is like manure” line by name. The rest of the post is about Virgin Unite, the Carbon War Room, The B Team, The Elders and the Giving Pledge.

author.heading: Who was Richard Branson?
author.metaLine: Born 18 July 1950 · English entrepreneur · co-founder of the Virgin Group
author.bio: Sir Richard Charles Nicholas Branson co-founded the Virgin Group in 1970, building it from a mail-order record business into an airline, rail, telecoms and spaceflight conglomerate. He is also an unusually prolific blogger: for years he posted short, plain-spoken pieces on Virgin.com, which is where this line first appeared. The post is a philanthropy piece rather than a business one — it runs through Virgin Unite, the Carbon War Room, The Elders and the Giving Pledge he and his wife Joan had signed.

misattribution.heading: Right author, borrowed joke
misattribution.intro: This is the unusual case: the attribution is correct. Branson wrote the sentences and published them under his own name. What travels with the quote and is not right is the assumption that the idea is his — and three older lines get swapped for it.

items.why: Bacon really did make the comparison, and much earlier. In “Of Seditions And Troubles” the text reads “And money is like muck, not good except it be spread” (Project Gutenberg ↗). Looser modern rewordings of that sentence circulate as Bacon quotations; Branson’s two-sentence version is not one of them.

items.tag: Quoted by Branson, not written by him
items.why: “Money is like manure; it’s not worth a thing unless it’s spread around encouraging young things to grow” is Dolly Levi’s line in The Matchmaker (1954), Act 4 (Wikiquote ↗). Branson quotes it by name directly after his own sentences, so the two get merged into one “Branson quote” — and occasionally Wilder’s line alone gets a Branson byline.

items.who: Clint Murchison Jr. and Clint Murchison Sr.
items.why: Time of 16 June 1961 quotes the Texas financier Clint Murchison Jr. passing on advice from his father: “Money is like manure. If you spread it around, it does a lot of good. But if you pile it up in one place, it stinks like hell” (TIME archive ↗). The two wordings are often confused.

Bacon did not claim the two-part form. Quote Investigator notes that in Apophthegmes New and Old Bacon credits a Mr. Bettenham with the version where riches in a heap gave a stench but spread upon the ground caused much fruit (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The quote is genuinely Branson’s wording, from his post “Why money is like manure” on Virgin.com, 13 February 2014 (archived original ↗) — but the analogy is centuries older, and Branson said so himself, crediting Wilder in his next breath.

context.heading: An old joke, retold by a billionaire
lead: Branson did not drop this line in a boardroom. It opens a short post about giving money away — Virgin Unite, the Carbon War Room’s Caribbean renewables work, drug-policy reform in Miami, The Elders in Iran, and the Giving Pledge he and his wife Joan had signed. The sentence before it is the setup: money, he writes, is like manure, and this might sound like he is full of it, but hear him out. The two sentences people quote are the punchline of a philanthropy argument, not a theory of capital.

What makes the line worth a page is that Branson was consciously passing on someone else’s joke. He names Thornton Wilder immediately after. And Wilder was not first either: Francis Bacon put “money is like muck, not good except it be spread” into his Essays, and Quote Investigator tracks the heap-and-stench version onward through King James I, English proverb collections, a 1961 Time profile of a Texas oilman, and finally to Branson. The saying survives because manure is the rare metaphor that carries both halves of the thought — useless when hoarded, productive when scattered.
context.detailsSummary: The closest ancestors, in Bacon’s own words and in Texas
detailsBody: The structure of Branson’s version — a stinking heap set against a beneficial spreading — is closer to a second Bacon text than to the famous Essays line. Quote Investigator points to Bacon’s Apophthegmes New and Old, where the two-part form is credited not to Bacon but to a “Mr. Bettenham”: riches heaped up gave a stench, but spread upon the ground caused much fruit.

The closest twentieth-century relative is Texan. Time of 16 June 1961 has Clint Murchison Jr. repeating advice from his father: money spread around does a lot of good, but piled up in one place it stinks like hell. That version and Branson’s are close enough in shape that the two are often confused.
